title: Let's Talk About FOMAT: Fear of Missing Agent Time — Michael Richman, Cmd+Ctrl

summary: Michael Richman, who leads several engineering teams at Bitly, co-wrote the Bitly MCP server, and co-leads AI coding tools strategy, introduces FOMAT (Fear of Missing Agent Time). The concept captures the frustration of agents sitting blocked waiting for input while the developer is away. As coding tasks scale from minutes to potentially days, the problem worsens—developers cannot predict when an agent will need them. Richman built Cmd+Ctrl (Command and Control) to address this gap, noting no solution existed when he started, though Anthropic recently released remote control features and Cursor introduced a related solution. Cmd+Ctrl is a mobile (iOS, Android) and web app that also works on Apple Watch. It provides three core capabilities: interacting with existing agent sessions from anywhere, starting new sessions remotely, and managing many sessions through subscriptions, push notifications, an on-my-radar section, and a recent-sessions view. An overview dashboard generates standup-style summaries using the last several messages of each session. The system is agent-agnostic, working with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and Open Code. Each agent runs alongside an open-source Cmd+Ctrl daemon that monitors lifecycle events and communicates with a central control plane. The control plane aggregates sessions across machines and frameworks, so a developer could have Claude Code on a Mac and Codex in a cloud VM visible through a single UI. Three video demos illustrate the workflow: (1) a Claude Code session started in terminal mirrors to the phone; the user subscribes for notifications, responds from the phone, receives a push notification on completion, and resumes in the terminal; (2) a new session is launched from the phone, continued in the terminal, and synchronized back; (3) session management shows thousands of sessions organized by category. Richman redefines flow for the agentic era as agent choreography—moving between multiple parallel agents—rather than traditional solo focus. He closes by emphasizing the high cognitive load and exhaustion of managing multiple agent sessions, referencing a Simon Wilson interview on Lenny's podcast, and arguing that breaks are when developers have their best ideas. Cmd+Ctrl aims to make agents reachable during those breaks wherever and whenever they occur, truly alleviating FOMAT. Richman invites the audience to try Cmd+Ctrl, share their workflows and pain points, and connect with him online.

sections.title: FOMAT: Fear of Missing Agent Time
sections.summary: Richman introduces FOMAT—the anxiety and lost productivity when agents sit blocked waiting for input while the developer is away. As task durations grow from minutes to hours or days, checking back periodically becomes insufficient; developers need to know exactly when an agent needs them and when it is done.

sections.title: Speaker Background and Motivation
sections.summary: Richman reintroduces himself: leads engineering teams at Bitly, co-leads AI coding tools strategy, co-wrote the Bitly MCP server, and trains engineers on AI skills. He built Cmd+Ctrl because he needed a way to work with coding agents outside the terminal or IDE and nothing existed yet, though Anthropic and Cursor have since released related solutions.

sections.title: Setup Overview and Demo 1: Session Interaction from Phone
sections.summary: Richman shows his multi-terminal, multi-agent setup and explains the difficulty of tracking more than 2-3 sessions. Demo 1 shows a Claude Code session started in terminal mirrored to the iPhone app; the user subscribes for notifications, sends a response from the phone, receives a push notification when the agent completes, and resumes seamlessly in the terminal.

sections.title: Demo 2: Starting New Sessions from Mobile
sections.summary: Demo 2 shows launching a new session from the Cmd+Ctrl mobile app, selecting from configured agents (Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor), switching directory, and issuing a prompt. The session is resumed in the terminal and continued bidirectionally. Richman notes he often starts sessions from bed in the morning.

sections.title: Demo 3: Session Management and Overview Dashboard
sections.summary: Demo 3 shows session management across thousands of sessions organized into push-notification subscriptions, on-my-radar, recent (last 24 hours), and the rest. An overview dashboard provides standup-style summaries of recent sessions using their last several messages.

sections.title: Architecture: Daemons, Control Plane, Open Source
sections.summary: Each agent platform runs a Cmd+Ctrl daemon alongside the agent that monitors lifecycle events and communicates with a central control plane. The control plane aggregates sessions regardless of machine or framework, providing a single pane of glass across dev machines and cloud VMs. The daemon layer is open source, allowing integration with custom agent frameworks.

sections.title: Agent Choreography and Time Away from Agents
sections.summary: Richman redefines coding flow for the agentic era as agent choreography—managing multiple parallel agents, unblocking and redirecting them—rather than traditional solo deep focus. He notes the always-available agent paradigm paradoxically highlights the value of time away from agents, referencing Matt Pocock's earlier talk.

sections.title: Closing: Cognitive Load, Breaks, and Call to Action
sections.summary: Richman highlights the high cognitive load and exhaustion of managing multiple agent sessions, referencing a Simon Wilson interview on Lenny's podcast. He argues that breaks are when developers have their best ideas and that systems like Cmd+Ctrl are needed to make agents reachable during those breaks wherever and whenever they occur, truly alleviating FOMAT. He closes by inviting the audience to try Cmd+Ctrl, share their workflows and pain points, and connect with him online.

Demo 3: Session management showing thousands of sessions organized by notification subscriptions, on-my-radar, recent, and rest sections; overview dashboard with standup summaries
